title: Patterns: regular expressions that earn their keep
objective: By the end of this lesson you can write the handful of regular expressions that answer most real questions, and you know when a pattern is the wrong tool.

blocks.text: You have used grep to find lines containing a word. A regular expression is the same idea with a shape instead of a fixed word: not "find failed" but "find something that looks like an IP address at the start of a line". Ten symbols cover almost everything you will actually need.

rows: Zero or more of what came before
ab+c matches abc but not ac
failed$ matches lines ending in failed

blocks.title: Use grep -E and stop escaping things
blocks.text: Plain grep uses an older dialect where +, ?, | and {} must be written with a backslash. grep -E uses the modern one where they do not. Reach for grep -E by default and your patterns will look like the ones in every tutorial and language you meet later.
Four patterns you will reuse constantly

blocks.caption: Worth memorising
lines: grep -E '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}' app.log      # lines starting with a date
grep -E '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' access.log  # anything shaped like an IPv4 address
grep -Ei 'error|fail|denied' app.log               # any of several words, case-insensitive

blocks.text: Flags that turn grep into an investigation tool

rows: Line numbers — so you can go straight there in an editor
Print only the matching part, not the whole line
Show 3 lines after / before / around each match
Print only the names of files that matched
Limit a recursive search to certain files

blocks.title: Context is what makes a log readable
blocks.text: An error line alone rarely explains itself. grep -C 3 shows you the three lines either side — what the system was doing before it failed and what it did next. In practice that is the difference between finding the error and understanding it.

blocks.caption: Combining them the way people actually do
lines: grep -rn --include='*.conf' 'password' /etc     # credentials sitting in config files
grep -C 3 'segfault' /var/log/syslog            # a crash with its surroundings
grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#  ^ pull out every IP, count them, rank them — the pipeline from the previous lesson

blocks.title: When a pattern is the wrong tool
blocks.text: Regular expressions match shapes in text; they do not understand structure. Parsing JSON, HTML, or nested configuration with a pattern works on your sample and breaks on the real file. When the data has structure, use a tool that knows that structure — jq for JSON, the service's own query command for its data.

blocks.title: Build up one pattern at a time
steps: Run: grep -c '' /var/log/syslog                          (how many lines you are dealing with)
Run: grep -En '^[A-Z][a-z]{2} [ 0-9]' /var/log/syslog | head   (lines starting with a date stamp)
Run: grep -C 2 -i error /var/log/syslog | head -30       (errors with their context)
Run: grep -rn 'PermitRootLogin' /etc/ssh/                (a specific setting, with line numbers)
blocks.expected: A count, then progressively sharper filters, then errors shown with the lines around them, and finally a configuration setting located by file and line — which is exactly how a real question gets answered.

cheatsheet: . any character · * zero or more · + one or more · ? optional
^ start of line · $ end of line · [abc] one of these · [0-9] a digit
{3} exactly three · {2,4} between two and four
Use grep -E so +, ?, | and {} work without backslashes
-n line numbers · -r recursive · -o only the match · -l only filenames
-C 3 shows three lines around each match — context makes logs readable
grep -oE 'pattern' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn ranks what appears most
Do not parse JSON or HTML with a pattern — use a tool that understands the structure

checkpoint.prompt: Which pattern matches lines that begin with three digits?
checkpoint.explanation: ^ anchors to the start of the line and {3} means exactly three repeats. The first option anchors to the end instead, and the third matches almost everything because * allows zero.

checkpoint.prompt: You found an error line in a log but it does not explain itself. What is the quickest next step?

choices.B: grep -C 3 to show the lines around it
choices.C: grep -c to count how often it happens
choices.D: grep -l to list the file names

checkpoint.explanation: Context lines show what happened immediately before and after — usually where the actual explanation is.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a regular expression a poor tool for reading a JSON configuration file?

choices.A: Patterns match shapes in text but do not understand nesting or structure
choices.C: JSON files are always too large

checkpoint.explanation: They work on your sample and break on real data. Structure needs a parser. jq understands JSON nesting; a pattern only sees characters in a line.

checkpoint.prompt: What does grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' access.log give you?

choices.A: The lines that do not contain an address
choices.B: Only the IPv4-shaped addresses themselves, one per match
choices.C: Every whole line that contains an IPv4-shaped address

checkpoint.explanation: -o prints just the matching portion rather than the full line, which is what makes it feedable into sort | uniq -c for counting.
